# The Map That Redraws Itself

At night, the city becomes a map folded inside darkness. Every lamp suggests a destination, though none asks for passengers. I begin walking without any compass, carrying only my curiosity. The pavement holds old memories beneath its thin forgiving skin. Streets cross like sentences, while their true destinations remain unclear. A grocery sign bleeds orange light across the wet stone. Somewhere nearby, a bus sighs at the edge of morning. Its doors open, revealing unfamiliar faces briefly washed with gold. I board, though the route has vanished from my mind. The driver nods, as if midnight were a legitimate passenger.

We travel through districts whose names I have already forgotten. Windows turn familiar buildings into silhouettes, then entirely loose abstractions. The empty seats hum softly, guarding the memories of crowds. Streetlights pass like beads strung upon a long dark necklace. Each block erases itself behind us, departing quietly without regret. I imagine the driver carrying invisible charts of the moon. He steers around potholes, distant thunder, and all my hesitation. A folded timetable rests beside his elbow, apparently completely useless. Still, its little printed squares resemble windows from another century. The bus climbs a hill and enters the uncharted part.

Beyond the depot, houses sit scattered like forgotten chess pieces. Their porch lights burn patiently against the slow coming rain. A woman waters small herbs beneath her open kitchen window. She mistakes my reflection for a neighbor unexpectedly awaiting news. I almost offer the news that I remain still alive. Instead, the old bus exhales softly and carries me onward. Rain begins tapping the roof with many tiny impatient fingers. The windows blur, and every distant light becomes a planet. We travel through a dark ocean disguised as ordinary asphalt. The driver turns toward a place absent from his map.

This street does not appear on any map I own. It curves around a warehouse that moonlight has painted blue. An abandoned station waits beneath a heavy canopy of branches. Rust climbs the old timetable as green ivy climbs stone. I get off right there, because certainty has become exhausting. The bus disappears around the bend, its red lamps fading. For a moment, the station platform feels like an island. Then a train arrives, completely silent and somehow impossibly punctual. Its doors open onto the waiting room of another century. Nobody steps aboard, and for this moment I remain outside.

I enter because that open doorway promises completely different weather. Inside, the old station clock has stopped at twelve seventeen. Dust furrows the long wooden benches like tiny dried rivers. A faded old schedule lists destinations that no country recognizes. I move toward the ticket window, where a bell rings. The attendant is gone, though her small coffee still steams. Steam fogs the glass, then slowly forms an unknown coastline. Beyond it, the silver rain erases the invisible city outside. I press my palm against the cool window, seeking meaning. The glass returns my face, suddenly older and less certain.

A distant train whistle calls from somewhere beyond the tracks. I follow it through a garden grown over with iron. Rails become tangled roots, while weeds become strange patient conductors. The platform ends, but the strange imagined journey continues anyway. I step onto soft grass that hides another buried map. Here, perhaps, this old forgotten station can rest at last. A fox watches from the hedge, bright-eyed and intensely curious. It disappears without leaving any tracks in the wet grass
